title: Cut a sound-out into sayable chunks
statement: Cut a word to be sounded out into two to four chunks, each sayable alone and as it sounds in the word, merging any lone schwa into a neighbour.
example: One taught word's three dictionary syllables became two chunks, because its schwa syllable cannot be said alone.
detail: A sounded-out word on a reading course's vocabulary card was reported to sound bad: chunks spelled like words of their own were read by the voice as those words, so the child heard pieces, not the word (`grade3-reading/.claude/skills/sound-out-respell/SKILL.md`, lines 10-12). The skill written in response chunks for the mouth, not the dictionary: each chunk must be sayable alone and sound like its slice of the word, a bare schwa or lone short-vowel syllable merges into its neighbour, and two to four chunks leave the voice fewer places to invent a word (lines 22-28). The printed chunks stay letter slices of the real spelling joined by hyphens, and stress goes into the voice's style note, not into capitals (lines 29-32).
against: An earlier rule in the course's rulebook makes the first pronunciation the dictionary syllable break: "the word's first pronunciation is the dictionary syllable break (nurs·er·y, en·chant·ing — every syllable has a vowel sound)" (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g3-reading/iteration-6/distilled/04-CONTENT-AUTHORING.md`, lines 407-408), and an external audit held that one word's two-part split "splits the word into two syllables instead of the correct three" (`grade3-reading/artifacts/feedback-inceptbench-2026-09-30/REGISTER.md`, line 65). The skill departs from the dictionary on purpose (`grade3-reading/.claude/skills/sound-out-respell/SKILL.md`, line 22).

evidence.quote: When a chunk is spelled as something the TTS reads as a word of its own ("merci" → French, "al" → Al, "a" → ay), the child hears pieces, not the word.

A chunk must be sayable alone AND sound like its slice of the word. A bare schwa or lone short vowel syllable never stands alone — merge it into its neighbour … Two to four chunks. Fewer chunks = fewer places for the TTS to invent a word.
Printed chunks are LETTER SLICES of the word joined by hyphens … Stress is spoken, not printed — put it in the style note (Step 3), not in capitals.
merge it into its neighbour: me·na·cing → mena · cing
